newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Spate of summits place Ukraine in central Europe.
newsitem.headline: Spate of summits place Ukraine in central Europe.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma returned to Kiev triumphant from meeting the Pope and European leaders after a whirlwind week consolidating Ukraine's place in central Europe -- though his message had trouble reaching the Vatican.

Independent Ukraine has grown in the shadows since breaking free of Moscow in 1991 and still has some way to go to raise its profile in the world -- its flag hung embarrassingly upside-down during Kuchma's trip to Poland to see John Paul II on Tuesday.

But analysts saw his meeting with the Pope -- whose theme was European unity -- and leaders of Poland, Germany, Hungary, the Czech and Slovak Republics and Lithuania as another chance for Kuchma to prove his central European credentials.

The high-point of Kuchma's diplomatic diary in recent days, which also included a summit in Estonia and a deal with NATO, was cutting another fibre of Ukraine's umbilical cord to Russia by ending the need for more squabbling over the Black Sea Fleet.
Kuchma hammered out a deal for Russia to keep its lion's share of the Fleet in Ukrainian docks for 20 years and on May 31 signed a friendship treaty with President Boris Yeltsin.
"It's been a very good week in the life of Ukraine -- the Tallinn summit, NATO, Russia, Romania and now the Pope," one Western diplomat in Kiev said.

Washington, so keen to promote Ukrainian independence from Moscow that Kiev is the third largest recipient of U.S. aid, welcomed the Russian-Ukrainian handshake. President Bill Clinton sent Kuchma a letter hailing a deal signed with Romania on Monday as making a big contribution to European unity.

So in one week Kuchma has managed not only to make friends with his neighbours but also to please Western partners concerned by economic problems and government corruption which have turned off several big investors in recent months.

Anxious to set up new strategic partnerships away from Russia and develop an independent foreign policy, Kuchma joined Poland's Aleksander Kwasniewski and the Baltic leaders in Estonia on May 27 to hail a historic pact signed between Russia and the NATO Western defence alliance the same day in Paris.
Two days later Ukraine initialled its own security pact with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), which will be signed when new members are invited to join in Madrid in July.
Then Kuchma and Romanian President Emil Constantinescu ended decades of mutual mistrust by signing a long-delayed treaty aimed at settling differences over World War Two-era borders.
Russia has now formally accepted Ukraine's territorial integrity by agreeing to pay rent at Sevastopol in Crimea.

And Kiev, hearing Moscow's insistence that former Soviet republics should not join NATO and realising it has no chance of joining the alliance in the short term anyway, has settled for a promise of "consultations" with the pact if it feels threatened.

Almost six years into independence, Ukraine has taken big steps towards creating a modern state -- a new constitution, democratically elected institutions and a peaceful handover of power to Kuchma from the country's first leader Leonid Kravchuk.
But Yeltsin's visit last week, postponed six times in as many years, was seen as one of the most significant moves.
The division of the Soviet Fleet and uncertainty about the status of Crimea has frayed nerves at home and abroad for years.

Politically, Russia paid by promising to ignore nationalists who claim Crimea while Ukraine paid by letting foreign forces officially stay on its soil. But some analysts saw an economic price for Ukraine, despite the fact that its debt to Russia was restructured in return for rent of Sevastopol.
Local media said Russia was free to increase its already massive role in the economy of its 51 million Slav neighbours.
"Recognising Ukraine's independence...will be accompanied by attempts to weaken its economic independence," Den daily wrote.

The paper was concerned Kuchma had not done more to boost Ukrainian industry especially in the energy sector, noting that Russian companies were still free to take part in a non-commercial tender at Ukraine's main oil processing plant.
Other concerns that the 20-year Russian navy lease on Sevastopol could hurt any future bid by Kiev to join NATO were set against the fact that the ships are obsolete anyway.
Kievskiye Vyedomosti daily concluded: "It's not all as gloomy as it seemed. And there's even a reason for optimism: at last we have learned to play with Russia as equals."
